case_scope.source_excerpt:
For a positive-temperature fixed-$V,n$ chart, write $\theta=T/T_*$. For a dimensionless real exponent $q\ge1$, the notation $C_V(T)=O(\theta^q)$ as $\theta\downarrow0$ means that there exist a constant $M>0$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ and a dimensionless $\delta\in(0,1]$ such that $|C_V(T)|\le M\theta^q$ whenever $0<\theta<\delta$. Finite convergence of the entropy integral alone does not imply such a bound for any real $q\ge1$, even when the entropy has a finite limit and the local response-chart identities apply. The displayed branch is a formal chart calculation, not a claim that a particular substance realizes the chart.

The displayed entropy is $S^{\rm SI}$ in physical SI coordinates. For this constructed local model, choose the positive-amount open neighborhood stated here (or any positive neighborhood of the fixed amount, extending this entropy independently of amount) and let $O_c$ be the numerical preimage of that product patch under $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n\,\mathrm{mol})$. Declare $O_c$ as the model's local state-domain patch and set $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$. The derivatives below are those of $S^{\rm SI}=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}$ on $\Phi_c(O_c)$, exactly as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. This supplies the numerical-to-SI chart identification for the formal witness, with no assertion of a measured material or a global constitutive extension.

Fix a constitution $c$ and an open dimensionless subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the single-phase region of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$, where $\Phi_c$ is the SI coordinate map defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. For fixed physical amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ with nonempty slice $\Omega_n:=\{(U,V):(U,V,n)\in\Omega\}$, this slice is open in $\mathbb R^2$. Use $T,p$ from [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] as functions of the physical coordinates on $\Omega_n$. For a response derivative, restrict to an open neighborhood in $\Omega_n$ where the required natural-coordinate map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open image, so its inverse expresses the physical $(U,V)$ as $C^1$ functions of those natural coordinates ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Specifically, $C_V$ uses $(U,V)\mapsto(T,V)$ at fixed $n$, while $C_p$, $\kappa_T$, and $\alpha_p$ use $(U,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ at fixed $n$. The existence of each such local chart is a hypothesis for its response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. Each derivative uses the indicated natural variables and holds all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c, d \in F$.

1. **Translation invariance.** If $a < b$ then $a + c < b + c$.
2. **Adding inequalities.** If $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in I$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the point $\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y$ belongs to $I$. The function $f$ is **convex** when the convex-combination inequality holds for every weight in $[0,1]$:

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

It is **strictly convex** when this inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<\lambda<1$. It is **concave** (respectively **strictly concave**) when $-f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). It is **midpoint convex** when the displayed inequality is required only at $\lambda=1/2$.
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $K=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$, which is noncompact: the open cover $U_n=(-1,-1/n)\cup(1/n,1)$ for $n\ge2$ has no finite subcover. Let $C=[-1,1]$ and use dimensionless coordinate $x$. For constants $s_0>a>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, define the ambient entropy extension and its restriction by
$$
\widetilde s(x)=s_0-a x^2\quad(x\in C),\qquad s=\widetilde s|_K.
$$
For $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$,
$$
\widetilde s((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y)+a t(1-t)(x-y)^2\ge(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y),
$$
so $\widetilde s$ is concave on the convex ambient domain. It is continuous, bounded, and positive since $s_0-a>0$. The admissible generator set $K$ excludes the maximizing point $x=0$. Declare all Borel probability measures on $K$ with fixed barycenter $\bar x=0$ feasible, with entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $y\in K$, define the point mass $\delta_y(A)=1$ if $y\in A$ and $0$ otherwise for every Borel set $A\subseteq K$. It is countably additive because at most one set in a disjoint family can contain $y$, and $\delta_y(K)=1$.

Let $K=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$, which is noncompact: the open cover $U_n=(-1,-1/n)\cup(1/n,1)$ for $n\ge2$ has no finite subcover. Let $C=[-1,1]$ and use dimensionless coordinate $x$. For constants $s_0>a>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, define the ambient entropy extension and its restriction by
$$
\widetilde s(x)=s_0-a x^2\quad(x\in C),\qquad s=\widetilde s|_K.
$$
For $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$,
$$
\widetilde s((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y)+a t(1-t)(x-y)^2\ge(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y),
$$
so $\widetilde s$ is concave on the convex ambient domain. It is continuous, bounded, and positive since $s_0-a>0$. The admissible generator set $K$ excludes the maximizing point $x=0$. Declare all Borel probability measures on $K$ with fixed barycenter $\bar x=0$ feasible, with entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $y\in K$, define the point mass $\delta_y(A)=1$ if $y\in A$ and $0$ otherwise for every Borel set $A\subseteq K$. It is countably additive because at most one set in a disjoint family can contain $y$, and $\delta_y(K)=1$.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has the fixed aggregate composition $\nu(a)=\nu_T$ of its declared type, using the amount-function interpretation in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $\nu_{T\times T'}=\nu_T+\nu_{T'}$, $\nu_{tT}=t\nu_T$, with $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$ and $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. Matching scalar masses alone do not identify aggregate composition. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{*\}$, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(*)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. Type permutations, reassociation, reversible identifications, and the identity $T\times1=T$ are part of the declared type structure. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

boundaries.evidence: Definition the optional unit has zero amount and only the empty compound as representation. Each simple chart is separately nonempty with positive bookkeeping weight; the unit is not a simple chart.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. Fix $T_0=300\,\mathrm K$, $p_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $g_0=1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $c>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\kappa>0$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. On a common open chart define
$$
g_i(T,p)=g_0-s_i(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_i(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
for $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, with $s_\alpha=2\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $s_\beta=5\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_\alpha=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, and $v_\beta=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Set $G_i=n_i g_i$ and use the natural Gibbs assignments $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. Thus same-tag homogeneity is explicit. Assume the constructed model stipulates an attained coexistence endpoint with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange, and a reversible $\alpha\to\beta$ conversion in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at $T_0$. The reversible conversion is a record of the complete finite isolated compound comprising converted phases, the fixed-temperature reservoir, work stores and all auxiliaries, with equilibrium endpoints and additive component entropy. Every component other than the converted phases and reservoir has zero entropy change, and the reservoir change is $-Q/T_0$. These are the exact additional entropy premises of the local Clapeyron theorem. These parameters and endpoint assumptions are model inputs, not empirical claims.

boundaries.evidence: Example the fixed molar-volume difference is three-thousandths cubic metres per mole, so its coexistence-slope denominator is nonzero. dT denotes a differential, not an unconstrained scalar divisor that must be nonzero.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $K=\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb R$ be the compact generator domain, with dimensionless coordinate $x$. On the convex ambient domain $[0,1]$, define the affine extension $\widetilde s(x)=s_0+a x$ and restrict it to $s=\widetilde s|_K$, where fixed $s_0,a>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. For $x,y\in[0,1]$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $\widetilde s((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y)$, so the extension is concave. Take the barycenter to be $\bar x=\tfrac12$ and declare every Borel probability mixture on $K$ with that barycenter feasible.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix a material constitution and amount $n$ and stipulate, on $U>0$ and $0<V<1/b$, the entropy chart

$$S(U,V)=C\ln(U/U_*)+aV-\frac{ab}{2}V^2+S_0,$$

where $C>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $U_*>0$ is in joules, $a>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $b>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and $S_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Consider a piecewise-C1 quasistatic cycle with isotherms $T_1>T_2>0$ and volumes $0<V_1<V_2<1/b$, joined by isochoric legs. The ideal frictionless piston load tracks the equilibrium pressure, controlled heat exchange is permitted along the path, and no other work coordinate acts. The calculation shows that the pressure-work integral is not an endpoint increment.

The displayed entropy is $S^{\rm SI}$ in physical SI coordinates. For this constructed local model, choose the positive-amount open neighborhood stated here (or any positive neighborhood of the fixed amount, extending this entropy independently of amount) and let $O_c$ be the numerical preimage of that product patch under $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n\,\mathrm{mol})$. Declare $O_c$ as the model's local state-domain patch and set $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$. The derivatives below are those of $S^{\rm SI}=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}$ on $\Phi_c(O_c)$, exactly as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. This supplies the numerical-to-SI chart identification for the formal witness, with no assertion of a measured material or a global constitutive extension.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $\beta,z>0$, and $b\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}$. On the simple labelled sector $\mathcal S_{L,N}=\{q\in\Lambda_L^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ use $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}(q)=\sum_{i<j}\phi(q_i-q_j)$ and the periodic energy $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For $N\geq1$ define
$$Z_b(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_{L,N}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_b(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, and put $\Xi_b(L,z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_b(L,N;\beta)$. The unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ has sector density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to labelled Lebesgue measure, so its normalized grand partition is
$$Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}]=e^{-L^d}\Xi_b(L,z,\beta).$$
The exact-$N$ canonical law $C^b_{L,N}$ has density $e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/(N!Z_b(L,N;\beta))$ on $\mathcal S_{L,N}$, and the grand-canonical law $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ has density $z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)$ relative to $Q_{\Lambda_L}$. Let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, and take $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$ under $C^b_{L,N_L}$. This is a statement about spatially averaged local observables through the empirical field, not about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin.

For $N\geq1$ define
$$Z_b(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_{L,N}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_b(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, and put $\Xi_b(L,z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_b(L,N;\beta)$. The unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ has sector density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to labelled Lebesgue measure, so its normalized grand partition is
$$Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}]=e^{-L^d}\Xi_b(L,z,\beta).$$
The exact-$N$ canonical law $C^b_{L,N}$ has density $e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/(N!Z_b(L,N;\beta))$ on $\mathcal S_{L,N}$, and the grand-canonical law $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ has density $z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)$ relative to $Q_{\Lambda_L}$. $$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with
stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. In fixed reference length and
energy units, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L]^d$ and define, for $N\ge1$,
$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for random variables $R,S,Y$ taking values in standard-Borel spaces $\mathcal R,\mathcal S,\mathcal Y$, with $R=r(S)$ for a measurable $r:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$, and a probability reference $Q_Y$ on $\mathcal Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)<\infty$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume the potential of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] is stable and regular. In addition, assume either (i) $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and nonincreasing, $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$, and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; or (ii) there is a hard-core radius $r_h>0$ such that $\phi(x)=+\infty$ whenever $|x|_\infty<r_h$. Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}h(N_{C_i}(\omega))-bN(\omega).$$
The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell. This is stronger than ordinary superstability and is not inferred from stability or regularity alone.

boundaries.evidence: Statement the near-core radius and positive core envelope determine positive subdivision scales. The h(N)/N^2 limit is taken through positive large N; zero occupation is handled by h(0)=0.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, and the full finite isolated compound (converted phases, reservoir, work stores and all auxiliaries) has equilibrium endpoints with additive component entropy, with every component other than the converted phases and that reservoir having zero entropy change, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. These are conditional model deductions. The slope conclusion is not asserted when $\Delta v=0$ or where the branch charts are not $C^1$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless generator coordinates. Each $x\in K$ labels one model-specified phase-generator state; the model assigns it entropy per mole $s(x)\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $s:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, using the numerical entropy value in that fixed unit. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ to be the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$. A Borel probability mixture is a countably additive probability measure $P$ on that sigma algebra; its barycenter and entropy per mole are the coordinatewise integrals $\int_Kx\,dP$ and $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. The nonnegative integral defined by
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] equals the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral
defined by [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], with the same value in
$[0,+\infty]$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: The map $h$ is continuous, so [L2] makes $H$ compact. For every Borel probability $P$ on $K$, each coordinate of $h$ is bounded and Borel. Compactness and [L1] give boundedness. If $|f|\le M$ for one such coordinate, [F3] gives $\int_K|f|\,dP\le M P(K)=M$, so $f$ is integrable.

Every point of $C$ is a finite convex combination of points $h(x_i)$. If such a representation has $N>d+2$, the linear map $T:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+2}$ defined by $T(c)=(\sum_i c_i h(x_i),\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector $c$ by [L3], because the coordinate bases give domain dimension $N$ and codomain dimension $d+2$. Thus $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i h(x_i)=0$, so $c$ has both positive and negative coordinates. After dropping zero weights from the representation, set $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace each weight $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. The new weights remain nonnegative, still sum to one, represent the same point, and at least one is zero. Repeating reduces every combination to at most $d+2$ terms. Hence $C$ is the image of $K^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$ under $\Theta((x_i),(\theta_i))=\sum_{i=1}^{d+2}\theta_i h(x_i)$, where $\Delta_{d+2}:=\{(\theta_i):\theta_i\ge0,\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; shorter combinations are padded with zero weights and any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Each factor $K$ is closed and bounded by [L2], and $\Delta_{d+2}$ is closed by continuity of the finite coordinate sum and its coordinate inequalities; it is bounded since $0\le\theta_i\le1$. Their product is therefore closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{(d+1)(d+2)}$, so compact by [L2]. To check $\Theta$ is continuous on this compact parameter set, fix a parameter $((x_i),(\theta_i))$. Each coordinate $h_j$ is bounded by some $M$ on $K$ and is continuous at each of the finitely many $x_i$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose neighborhoods of the $x_i$ making $|h_j(x_i')-h_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/(2N)$ for every output coordinate $j$, and require $|\theta_i'-\theta_i|<\epsilon/(2N(M+1))$. Since $0\le\theta_i'\le1$ and $|h_j(x_i)|\le M$, each product difference $|\theta_i'h_j(x_i')-\theta_ih_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/N$; summing over $i$ makes each output-coordinate difference smaller than $\epsilon$. Thus $\Theta$ is continuous. The continuous-image clause of [L2] makes its image $C$ compact, and [L2] also makes $C$ closed.

Fix any Borel probability $P$ on $K$ and let $y(P):=(\int_K x\,dP,\int_Ks\,dP)=\int_Kh\,dP$, with coordinatewise integration. For $\epsilon>0$, compactness of $H$ gives a finite cover of $H$ by open Euclidean balls of radius $\epsilon$. Their preimages under $h$ are Borel; disjointifying them in a fixed finite order gives a finite Borel partition $(A_i)$ of $K$. For every nonempty part choose $z_i\in A_i$ and put $\theta_i=P(A_i)$. Then $y_\epsilon:=\sum_i\theta_i h(z_i)$ belongs to $C$. For $x\in A_i$, both $h(x)$ and $h(z_i)$ lie in the same radius-$\epsilon$ ball, so each coordinate difference is at most $2\epsilon$. The simple map equal to $h(z_i)$ on $A_i$ has integral $y_\epsilon$ by the simple-integral definition. By linearity and the integral triangle inequality in [F3], each coordinate of $y(P)-y_\epsilon$ has absolute value at most $2\epsilon\sum_iP(A_i)=2\epsilon$. Consequently $\|y(P)-y_\epsilon\|_2\le2\epsilon\sqrt{d+1}$, so the sequence obtained with $\epsilon=1/n$ converges to $y(P)$. Since $C$ is closed by step 2.1, $y(P)\in C$.

Because $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, a finite convex combination of generators has barycenter $\bar x$; its corresponding combination of points $h(x)$ shows that $E_{\bar x}:=\{r\in\mathbb R:(\bar x,r)\in C\}$ is nonempty. The set $E_{\bar x}$ is bounded because $C$ is bounded, and it is closed because $C$ is closed and $r\mapsto(\bar x,r)$ is continuous. By [L2] it is compact in $\mathbb R$, so [L1] applied to the identity function yields a maximum $r_*\in E_{\bar x}$.

Represent $(\bar x,r_*)\in C$ by a finite convex combination $\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i(x_i,s(x_i))$, dropping zero weights. If $N>d+1$, the linear map $R:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ given by $R(c)=(\sum_i c_ix_i,\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector by [L3], since its domain dimension is $N$ and its codomain dimension is $d+1$. Hence $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_ix_i=0$, with both signs among the $c_i$. If $\sum_i c_is(x_i)\ne0$, choose the sign of $c$ so that this sum is positive. For sufficiently small $t>0$, the weights $\theta_i+tc_i$ are nonnegative, preserve total mass and barycenter, and increase the last coordinate above $r_*$, contradicting maximality in step 4.1. Thus $\sum_i c_is(x_i)=0$. Now take $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. This removes at least one positive weight while preserving total mass, barycenter, and entropy value $r_*$. Repeating finitely many times leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights.

Let $P_*:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ be the probability measure from step 5.1. Each $\delta_{x_i}$ is countably additive because among disjoint Borel sets at most one contains $x_i$, and $\delta_{x_i}(K)=1$; hence $P_*$ is a Borel probability measure. It has barycenter $\bar x$ and entropy $r_*$, so it is feasible by the model assumption. For any other feasible Borel probability $P$, step 3.1 gives $(\bar x,\int s\,dP)\in C$, so $\int s\,dP\le r_*$. Thus $P_*$ attains the entropy maximum among all Borel mixtures and has at most $d+1$ atoms. No finite generator menu was assumed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB, as required by the current variational-pressure supplier. Let $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, and assume $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable. Require the exact superstable regular hypotheses of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for this dimensionless potential: a stable part plus a nonnegative core part bounded below by a positive constant on an $\ell^\infty$-ball, with the supplier's lower and upper regular tail conditions. Use $\widehat H=H/E_0$, $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta$ for $\beta>0$, and $\widehat e=e/E_0$; then $\beta H=\widehat\beta\widehat H$. For this supplier convention, let $\nu$ be the supremum of finite-entropy, finite-energy attainable densities for $\widehat\varphi$, and write $\widehat\Phi(P)$ for the supplier's limiting positional energy density; let $e_0(\rho)=\inf\{\widehat\Phi(P):\rho(P)=\rho,\ I(P)<\infty\}$ be its numerical positional-energy infimum. Let $D\subset[0,\infty)$ be a nondegenerate density interval, and require $\inf D<\nu$ and $\widehat e>\inf_{\rho\in D}e_0(\rho)$. Use the supplier's periodic cubes $\Lambda_n$ of numerical volume $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$ and define explicitly
$$A_n=\{\omega:N_{\Lambda_n}(\omega)/V_n\in D,\ H_{n,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)/(E_0V_n)\le\widehat e\},\qquad \widehat e=e/E_0.$$
Here $H_{n,\mathrm{per}}$ is the physical positional energy in joules in the same periodic convention; equivalently its event inequality is $H_{n,\mathrm{per}}/V_n\le e$. For every $n$ with positive event probability, the prepared law is $R_n(B)=Q_{\Lambda_n}(B\cap A_n)/Q_{\Lambda_n}(A_n)$ on the finite count sigma-algebra. Equivalently, with $M_n=\sum_{N\ge0}\mu_{\Lambda_n,N}$, $R_n(B)=M_n(B\cap A_n)/M_n(A_n)$, since $Q_{\Lambda_n}=e^{-V_n}M_n$; use the count-sigma restriction of these positional measures. This defines the density-interval/upper-energy conditional preparation and its conditioned laws. For $\beta>0$, the finite-volume grand and microcanonical weights are those of [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]]. For $\beta=0$, require a nonempty hard-core displacement set and use the formal retained-admissibility continuation of [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]]; do not interpret $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For both the positive-$\beta$ branch and the formal retained-hard-core $\beta=0$ branch, [[thm-tdmath-interval-event-ensemble-limit]] gives eventual event positivity, the constrained entropy-rate limit, and common-minimizer accumulation points; at $\beta=0$, [[thm-tdmath-retained-hard-zero-beta-limit]] identifies the matching retained grand law and minimizer set. If the relevant common minimizer set is the singleton adopted in [[post-td-grand-variational-phase-uniqueness]] for the multiplier pair supplied by that branch, both the conditioned laws and the corresponding periodic grand laws converge locally to $P^\ast$ for every measurable local observable $f$ with $|f|\leq c(1+N_A)$ on a bounded region $A$. This is an interval-density and upper-energy result, not a fixed-particle-number or shrinking-shell theorem.


Here local observables are evaluated on the periodic continuation of the prepared torus configuration. This is the same periodic boundary preparation, with no new physical sampling assumption; a configuration is not extended by the empty configuration outside its fundamental cube.

Assume AC and $T>0$, with $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$. Under the stable regularly tempered positional model of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]] and the adopted ensemble weights of [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]], assume the dimensionless potential $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$ is Borel measurable as required by the current mathematical carriers. Set $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta$; write $F(\rho,\beta)$ and $P(\alpha,\beta)$ for the mathematical rates evaluated at $\widehat\beta$. Let $F(\rho,\beta)$ be the canonical log-partition rate per dimensionless reference volume, defined on interior attainable densities by the fixed-density limit and extended to the closed effective density domain by the upper-semicontinuous concave extension specified in [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]]. Let
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{V\to\infty}V^{-1}\log\sum_{N\geq0}e^{\alpha N}Z(V,N),\qquad \alpha=\log z.$$
Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{F(\rho,\beta)+\alpha\rho\},\qquad F(\rho,\beta)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\{P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\}.$$
In physical units, $p=(k_BT/\ell_0^d)P$ and the positional Helmholtz free-energy density is $f_{\mathrm{pos}}=-(k_BT/\ell_0^d)F$, with the fixed reference normalization of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. This duality concerns limiting thermodynamic functions only. It does not imply local ensemble equivalence, uniqueness of a phase, or convergence at excluded density endpoints.

Assume the entropy of each phase is $C^2$ on its physical state chart and its derivative-defined temperature at the endpoint is finite and positive. The equation-set dimension below concerns this smooth interior state only.

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of named species, $P\ge1$ the number of coexisting phase branches, and $R\ge0$ the number of independent internal reaction directions. Consider an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For each phase $\alpha$, use an intensive phase branch from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and an interior composition $x^\alpha\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}$. Let each branch chemical-potential map
$$
\mu^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)=(\mu_1^\alpha,\ldots,\mu_C^\alpha)
$$
be $C^1$ on a common open domain
$$
\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times(\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ})^P \subseteq\mathbb R^{\,n},\qquad n=2+P(C-1).
$$
Assume energy, volume, and every named species can be exchanged between every phase pair in both directions, and every listed reaction direction is feasible in both extent directions in every phase while that phase's energy, volume, other reaction extents, and all other phase coordinates are held fixed at the coexistence point. Let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent, dimensionless stoichiometric vectors, with extents measured in moles. Phase equilibrium imposes $\mu_i^\alpha-\mu_i^1=0$ for $1\le i\le C$, $2\le\alpha\le P$; internal reaction equilibrium imposes $(\nu^r)^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha=0$ in every phase for $1\le r\le R$. On the phase-equality locus these are the same $R$ equations in each phase, so count them once using phase 1. Put $q:=C(P-1)$ and $m:=q+R$. If $m=0$ (equivalently $P=1,R=0$), no equation is imposed and the local zero set is the whole chart, of dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2-R$. If $m\ge1$ and the combined equation map has an invertible $m\times m$ derivative minor at the solution, with $m\le n$, then the local zero set of these first-order coexistence-and-affinity equations is a graph of dimension
$$
n-q-R=C-P+2-R.
$$
This is the dimension of the equation zero set in intensive coordinates only; phase amounts and their extensive conservation constraints are not counted, and the actual stable-coexistence set may be a proper subset after additional stability constraints. If the nonsingular-minor condition fails, no dimension formula is asserted.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. On a noncomplete measure space an arbitrary almost-everywhere representative need not be measurable, so no integral of such a nonmeasurable $f$ is asserted.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.
